query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Ti to the NbMoTaW alloy will improve its room-temperature ductility by enhancing grain boundary cohesion while preserving the BCC solid‐solution matrix that yields high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, low atomic percentage of Titanium (e.g., 1–5 at.% Ti) into the NbMoTaW alloy (forming a NbMoTaW+Ti alloy) using the same processing route as the baseline to maintain a single-phase BCC structure.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be synthesized under similar vacuum arc melting or SLM conditions as the baseline. Mechanical testing will be performed at room temperature (to assess ductility) and at 1600 °C (to verify high-temperature yield strength). Irradiation testing will be conducted under conditions similar to those used in the first-principles studies to assess defect behavior and damage tolerance.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary cohesion due to Ti segregation and possible local alteration of dislocation core properties in the BCC matrix
generation.mechanism: The addition of Ti is expected to modify the local atomic bonding—especially at grain boundaries—reducing the nucleation of brittle fracture and facilitating dislocation activity at room temperature. This microstructural adjustment improves ductility without disrupting the high-temperature stability or the irradiation resistance inherent to the BCC NbMoTaW matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti-doped alloy will exhibit significantly improved room-temperature ductility compared to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline, while showing similar high yield strength at 1600 °C and retaining the irradiation resistance established by first-principles calculations. (The exact magnitude of ductility improvement is uncertain and will depend on the optimized Ti concentration.)
generation.baseline: Untreated, equal-atomic NbMoTaW with very poor room-temperature ductility but excellent yield strength at 1600 °C and irradiation resistance as predicted by earlier calculations.
generation.boundary: The Ti content must remain low (around 1–5 at.%) and uniformly distributed so that no secondary phases form; the processing route must maintain the single-phase BCC structure. Deviations in processing or composition that lead to phase instability would compromise the hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The precise improvement in ductility and the upper limit of tolerable Ti addition without affecting high-temperature performance are not well established and will require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaW alloys with varying Ti contents (e.g., 0, 1, 3, and 5 at.% Ti) using identical processing conditions that yield a single-phase BCC structure. Perform mechanical tests at room temperature to measure ductility (e.g., compression/tensile strain before fracture), at 1600 °C to assess yield strength, and subject samples to controlled irradiation (matching the parameters used in prior first-principles studies) while monitoring defect evolution via microscopy.
measurements: Room-temperature strain-to-failure or compressive plastic strain
Irradiation-induced defect density and hardening (using TEM and hardness testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility relative to the baseline or if the high-temperature yield strength or irradiation resistance degrades significantly compared to the untreated NbMoTaW alloy, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years []. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co []. First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [,]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 []. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [] and yield strength σ0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [].
